body.p: We thank the reviewer for the careful evaluation of our work and for recognizing the novelty and potential therapeutic implications of the relationship among intracrine signaling, inflammation, and NAD metabolism in meibomian gland dysfunction. We also appreciate the reviewer’s constructive comments on the limitations of the present study and areas for improvement in the manuscript.

Regarding the lack of information on meibomian gland health, tear film, and ocular surface, we have added a limitations section to explicitly acknowledge that these functional outcomes were not directly assessed in the present study. As the reviewer kindly noted, we only focused on a key pathological hallmark of MGD, namely age-associated tissue atrophy, and based on this we explored the NAD/3β-HSD/inflammation-mediated mechanism. Thus, a limitation of the present study is the lack of assessment of the downstream consequences of MGD. This point is now explicitly discussed in the manuscript; please note that additional details are provided in our responses to Reviewer #2’s Recommendations for the authors.

Regarding the human data, we added two additional human eyelid samples, increasing the sample size of the older group from 2 to 4. Nevertheless, we agree that the sample size remains limited and have now explicitly acknowledged this limitation in Discussion as follows:

“A caveat of this study is that the number of human eyelid samples analyzed was limited. Larger human cohorts will be necessary to establish the translational relevance of the age-associated CD38 accumulation observed in human tissues.”
Taken together, we believe that these revisions have clarified the scope and limitations of our present study.

disp-quote.p: Summary:

The authors aimed to investigate whether disruption of intracrine steroid hormone metabolism contributes to meibomian gland dysfunction and proposed a "vicious cycle" of gland dysfunction and inflammation, using a global Had3b6 knockout mouse model. The work addresses an important aspect of MGD, but its impact may be limited unless the intracrine mechanism can be more clearly distinguished from systemic hormonal effects.
Strengths:

This study addressed an important question. The hormonal regulation of the meibomian gland has long been recognized. If clarified, the concept of local steroid metabolism influencing gland homeostasis could have implications for understanding disease mechanisms and identifying therapeutic targets.
Weaknesses:

The use of a global knockout makes it difficult to separate local intracrine effects from systemic hormonal changes, and key controls and hormone measurements are lacking. LPS-induced inflammation may not reflect the chronic nature of MGD.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful evaluation of our work and for highlighting the importance of distinguishing local intracrine mechanisms from systemic hormonal effects. In response, we performed several additional experiments and substantially revised the manuscript. Specifically, we measured plasma testosterone and aldosterone levels and found no significant differences between Hsd3b6−/− and Hsd3b6+/+ mice. In addition, we repeated key experiments in castrated mice and observed that the effects of Hsd3b6 deletion on tarsal plate Cd38 expression and meibomian NAD levels were preserved despite the absence of testicular testosterone. These new findings provide additional support for a local intracrine mechanism in the eyelid. We also revised the Introduction and Discussion to better explain the proposed intracrine–inflammation vicious cycle and clarified the rationale and limitations of the LPS-based inflammation model, including its inability to fully recapitulate the chronic low-grade inflammation characteristic of MGD. Further details are provided in our responses to Reviewer #3’s Recommendations for the authors. We hope that these additions and revisions have strengthened the manuscript and addressed the reviewer’s concerns.

disp-quote.p: Overall, the authors need to provide bulk RNA sequencing data for all treatment groups and provide some explanation of the measurements in individual mice for gland growth.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. We have now replaced the original supplementary file with a complete RNA-seq dataset that includes all treatment groups (Supplementary Data 2). In addition, as described in our response to the Public Review comment above, we extensively revised our manuscript to provide explanation of gene expression profiles (particularly, representative meibum lipid-related genes) in the dataset.
Accordingly, we have expanded the Results and reconstructed the Discussion by incorporating two new discussion paragraphs. The relevant revisions are provided below for your perusal:

“… Furthermore, representative meibum lipid-related genes, including Awat2, Far2, Soat1, Plin2, and Scd1, exhibited a coordinated increase following 78c-NMN treatment (Fig. S5). While the changes in individual genes were modest and did not reach statistical significance (Fig. 4E), analysis of the gene set as a whole demonstrated a significant overall increase compared with vehicle-treated controls.”

“In contrast, the same treatment in young mice did not significantly alter gene expression profiles (Fig. 4E, young), and no coordinated increase was observed for Awat2, Far2, Soat1, Plin2, or Scd1 (Fig. S5). This result is consistent with previous studies [44,47,48] showing that 78c (or NMN) exerts minimal effects in young mice compared with aged mice across multiple physiological parameters, including glucose homeostasis, exercise tolerance, and cardiac function.”

“Although 78c+NMN treatment effectively restored meibomian gland size, the molecular mechanisms underlying this recovery remain incompletely understood. Treatment with 78c+NMN significantly increased the expression of Elovl4, Elovl7, and Hsd3b6. However, representative meibum lipid-related genes, including Awat2, Far2, Soat1, Plin2, and Scd1, exhibited only a modest coordinated increase following treatment. Interestingly, the expression of Pparg, a key transcriptional regulator of meibocyte differentiation and lipid synthesis [88-90], remained unchanged. These findings suggest that restoration of meibomian gland size by 78c+NMN does not require detectable changes in Pparg mRNA expression, although Pparg activity may instead be regulated at the level of protein abundance, subcellular localization, and/or post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation or SUMOylation [88,91].

Our previous transcriptomic analysis of FACS-purified meibomian gland basal acinar cells (meibomian precursor cells expressing androgen receptors) from Hsd3b6−/− mice demonstrated impaired expression of genes involved in cell proliferation and differentiation despite relatively preserved expression of lipid-related genes [6]. In contrast, a recent single-cell study showed that Pparg expression progressively increases during meibocyte differentiation, although it is already detectable in basal acinar cells [92]. These observations suggest that Hsd3b6-dependent intracrine activity primarily supports the maintenance and proliferation of basal acinar cells, whereas the canonical Pparg pathway predominantly regulates subsequent meibocyte differentiation and lipid synthesis. Together, these findings suggest that Hsd3b6-dependent intracrine activity contributes to meibomian gland homeostasis through mechanisms that complement the Pparg-associated pathway. Thus, our findings extend the current framework by indicating that meibomian gland homeostasis is maintained not only through canonical PPARγ-mediated regulation but also through intracrine steroidogenesis.”

disp-quote.p: The main suggestion for the study is the correlation with meibomian gland function. While the study correlates changes with 3B-HSD activity, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and NAD cofactor levels, there is little support describing the pathological changes to the meibomian glands and the impact on the tear film and ocular surface. The changes in the lipid profiles, tear film stability, aqueous tear production, ocular surface staining properties, corneal epithelial transcriptional abnormalities, and leukocyte infiltration into the corneal stroma could all be assessed. While the authors have done a thorough job of demonstrating the correlation of the three major factors listed above, the correlation with meibomian gland function is not completely assessed in the study.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that functional assessments such as tear film stability, ocular surface pathology, lipid composition, and other downstream manifestations of MGD would complement the mechanistic findings reported here and provide additional insight into their physiological consequences.

However, the primary objective of the present study was to define the molecular mechanism underlying MGD, specifically the pathological interaction between meibomian gland intracrine activity and inflammation, and the role of the CD38–NAD axis in this process. Accordingly, our experiments were designed to focus on mechanistic endpoints directly related to this hypothesis, including 3β-HSD activity, NAD availability, inflammatory gene expression, and CD38 accumulation. In addition, we assessed a key pathological hallmark of MGD, namely age-associated meibomian gland atrophy and its recovery following 78c/NMN treatment.

While direct evaluation of tear film and ocular surface parameters was beyond the scope of the present mechanistic study, we agree that such analyses represent important future directions. To acknowledge this, we have added the following statement to the Discussion:

“… Firstly, while this study focused on defining the molecular and structural mechanisms underlying meibomian gland dysfunction, functional outcomes such as tear film stability, ocular surface integrity, meibum lipid composition, and other clinically relevant manifestations of disease were not directly assessed. Given the well-established link between meibomian gland dysfunction and tear film instability [57-59], future studies incorporating these functional assessments will be important to determine how the molecular and structural changes identified here contribute to ocular surface pathology and disease progression.”

disp-quote.p: The description of the vicious cycle seemed a bit out of place in the introduction. This would have been most appropriate in the conclusion/discussion in the manuscript. The general nature of the description lacked focus on the eyelids and meibomian glands, and the narrative took time to get to the interactions that would be assessed in the study.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. We agree that the original Introduction placed excessive emphasis on the general concept of vicious cycles and that the discussion of disease-wide examples diverted attention from the specific focus of the present study on the meibomian gland.

In response, we substantially shortened and refocused the Introduction. Specifically, we removed the broad descriptions of vicious cycles in neurodegenerative, metabolic, and cardiovascular diseases. The revised Introduction now introduces the concept of a vicious cycle only briefly and moves more directly to the biological context of meibomian gland dysfunction and local intracrine steroidogenesis.

At the same time, we agree that the broader implications of this concept are better suited for the Discussion. We therefore added a brief concluding paragraph to discuss how our findings may inform the understanding of age-associated vicious-cycle processes in other diseases and may also provide a framework for considering intracrine-related pathology beyond the meibomian gland. The corresponding text has been added to the Discussion, as follows.

“Finally, although the present study focused on the eyelid meibomian gland, the concept of an intracrine–inflammation vicious cycle may have broader relevance. Self-reinforcing pathological processes are implicated in several age-associated diseases, and altered intracrine activity has been described in multiple extra gonadal and cancerous tissues [5,7,8,93,94]. Our findings may therefore provide a useful framework for understanding how local hormone metabolism contributes to the initiation and maintenance of tissue-specific pathological cycles during ageing.”

disp-quote.p: (1) Introduction:

(a) The first paragraph of the introduction defines the term "vicious cycle," but its relevance to the current study is low. It is not until line 54 that the specific tissue of interest is introduced. It is suggested that the beginning of the introduction be shortened to emphasize information that is directly relevant to the study.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We agree that the original opening of the Introduction was too general and that the specific focus of the study on the meibomian gland should be introduced earlier.

In response, we substantially shortened the first part of the Introduction. Specifically, we removed the broad discussion of vicious cycles across multiple disease contexts and revised the opening so that the concept of a vicious cycle is introduced only briefly. The revised Introduction now moves directly to the relevance of local intracrine steroidogenesis in the eyelid meibomian gland, thereby better emphasizing the biological context and focus of the present study.

At the same time, we recognized that some of the broader implications of the study remain important. Therefore, we incorporated these points into the Discussion, where we briefly discuss the potential relevance of intracrine–inflammation vicious cycles to other age-associated diseases and intracrine-related pathologies beyond the meibomian gland, as follows:

“Finally, although the present study focused on the eyelid meibomian gland, the concept of an intracrine–inflammation vicious cycle may have broader relevance. Self-reinforcing pathological processes are implicated in several age-associated diseases, and altered intracrine activity has been described in multiple extragonadal and cancerous tissues [5,7,8,93,94]. Our findings may therefore provide a useful framework for understanding how local hormone metabolism contributes to the initiation and maintenance of tissue-specific pathological cycles during ageing.”

disp-quote.p: (b) In the introduction, the authors should also include common types of intracrine hormones, such as DHT.

body.p: We thank the reviewer again for this valuable suggestion. In response, we revised the Introduction to include representative examples of intracrine steroid hormones, including 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and estrogens, together with a brief description of their local production and action within peripheral tissues. We believe that this addition helps clarify the concept of intracrinology for readers less familiar with the field.

“Common examples of intracrine steroid hormones include 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT) produced in the skin, prostate, and eyelid meibomian glands, as well as estrogens synthesized within the breast and endometrium [3-8]. These locally produced hormones act within the tissue in which they are synthesized.”

disp-quote.p: (c) The hypothesis of a "vicious cycle" in MGD is not fully explained. Specifically, how intracrine steroids drive the meibomian gland into a vicious cycle is not described. The current information only discusses a possible association between steroid hormones and meibomian gland health.

body.p: According to this important suggestion, we performed additional experiments and rewrote our introduction. Please note that plasma testosterone levels were not impaired in Hsd3b6−/− mice and their eyelid proinflammatory phenotypes (compared to wt mouse eyelid) remained preserved in castrated mice. These data are now provided, by performing additional experiments (please see our replies to your comments, below). Taking these observations into account, we have tempered our introduction.

disp-quote.p: (2) Results:

(a) One major concern is that sex hormones have long been recognized to be associated with the meibomian gland and have been extensively studied (see the TFOS guidelines). There have also been clinical trials using androgens to treat MGD. With the global knockout of Had3b6, systemic sex hormone levels could also be altered, which may result in MGD (estrogens are synthesized from androgens and would therefore also be affected).

body.p: This thoughtful concern is well received, as we were not attentive to describe systemic testosterone in Hsd3b6+/+ and Hsd3b6−/− mice in our original manuscript (for which we should apologize). The corresponding plasma testosterone data are now incorporated as Fig. S1A and presented below for your perusal.

Importantly, plasma testosterone levels in Hsd3b6−/− mice were comparable with those in wt Hsd3b6+/+ mice, consistent with the known compensatory role of the paralogous enzyme Hsd3b1 in the mouse testis [21], which was confirmed to be expressed in Hsd3b6−/− mice (see new Fig. S1B). This type of compensation by paralogous steroidogenic enzymes has also been reported in other knockout model, such as Hsd17b3−/− mice, in which circulating testosterone levels were preserved due to a compensatory role of Hsd17b12 in the testis (new refs [83,84]). Based on these results, we rewrote our Results and Discussion, as follows.

“plasma testosterone levels were indistinguishable between Hsd3b6−/− and Hsd3b6+/+ mice (Fig. S1A), consistent with the known compensatory role of the paralogous enzyme Hsd3b1 in the mouse testis [21], which was confirmed to be expressed in Hsd3b6−/− mice (Fig. S1B). These results indicate that local steroidogenic activity in the eyelid exerts anti-inflammatory effects independent of circulating testosterone levels.”

“For the interpretation of our meibomian intracrine activity model, it is important to note that in Hsd3b6−/− mice, plasma testosterone levels were maintained at the levels comparable with those in Hsd3b6+/+ mice (Fig. S1A). This appears due to a redundant expression of Hsd3b1 in the testis [6], although in the meibomian gland, Hsd3b6 is the sole enzyme (Fig. S1B) and accordingly its deletion causes the complete abolition of meibomian 3β-HSD activity [6]. The resilience of plasma testosterone levels has also been reported in a knockout mouse model deficient in Hsd17b3, a member of 17-ketosteroid reductase enzyme family required for the formation of testosterone [83], likely due to a potential compensatory role of the paralogous enzyme Hsd17b12 in the testis [84]. The Hsd3b6−/− vs. Hsd3b6+/+ phenotypes in the tarsal plate Cd38 expression and meibomian NAD levels were preserved in castrated mice (Fig. 2C, F), which provide additional evidence to support that non-systemic local steroidogenic activity in the eyelid, rather than circulating testicular testosterone, underlies the phenotypes observed in Hsd3b6−/− mice.”

- For context, please note that plasma testosterone levels showed substantial inter-individual variability in both genotypes. Such variability is a well-established physiological feature of male mice, reflecting episodic testosterone secretion. Indeed, classical studies showed that variation in testosterone levels within the same mouse sampled on different occasions is comparable to that observed between individual mice, and a recent longitudinal LC–MS/MS study confirmed 10- to 100-fold fluctuations within individual adult male mice (Bartke and Dalterio, 1975, PMID: 1216260; Kettering et al., 2026, PMID: 41880754). Thus, the variability observed in our dataset is consistent with the known physiological dynamics of circulating testosterone in male mice.

disp-quote.p: (b) To support the hypothesis of intracrine regulation in MGD, the following would be essential:
- a local or targeted knockout model, and
- a global knockout with appropriate controls, such as Had3b6+/+ mice combined with gonadectomy.
Otherwise, the current study reflects the role of general steroid hormones in the meibomian gland rather than an intracrine-specific mechanism.

body.p: We repeated our experiments using castrated Hsd3b6−/− mice. As shown in new Fig. 2C, we observed a significant increase in Cd38 expression in the tarsal plate of Hsd3b6−/− mice (n = 6, castrated) as compared to Hsd3b6+/+ control mice (n = 4, castrated). In addition, in Fig. 2F, we observed a significant decrease in NAD levels in the meibomian gland of Hsd3b6−/− mice (n = 3, castrated) as compared to Hsd3b6+/+ control mice (n = 5, castrated). These results provide additional evidence to support that local steroidogenic activity in the eyelid, rather than circulating testicular testosterone, underlies the phenotypes observed in Hsd3b6−/− mice. Based on these results and consideration, we have modified our manuscript as follows.
“… This difference was also observed in castrated mice; thus, the effect of Hsd3b6 deletion on Cd38 expression is independent of testicular testosterone (Fig. 2C).”
“… Note that regardless of castration, Hsd3b6 deletion reduced meibomian gland NAD levels.”

“…The Hsd3b6−/− vs. Hsd3b6+/+ phenotypes in the tarsal plate Cd38 expression and meibomian NAD levels were preserved in castrated mice (Fig. 2C, F), which provide additional evidence to support that non-systemic local steroidogenic activity in the eyelid, rather than circulating testicular testosterone, underlies the phenotypes observed in Hsd3b6−/− mice.”

disp-quote.p: (c) With the knockout of Had3b6, other steroid hormones may also be altered systemically, such as increased synthesis of the mineralocorticoid aldosterone. These hormonal changes could cause systemic effects such as hypertension, with unknown consequences for the meibomian gland. Please provide data on systemic steroid hormone levels to better interpret the current findings.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. To address the possibility that systemic mineralocorticoid alterations contribute to the observed meibomian gland phenotypes, we measured plasma aldosterone levels in Hsd3b6−/− and Hsd3b6+/+ mice. These new data are now included as Fig. S6.

Importantly, plasma aldosterone levels were not significantly different between Hsd3b6−/− and Hsd3b6+/+ mice (Fig. S6). This finding is consistent with the known expression pattern of steroidogenic enzymes in the adrenal zona glomerulosa, where both Hsd3b1 and Hsd3b6 are redundantly expressed and contribute to aldosterone biosynthesis (refs. 85-87). Thus, similar to the compensatory role of Hsd3b1 in maintaining systemic testosterone production in the testis, the redundant expression of Hsd3b1 in aldosterone-producing cells likely preserves systemic aldosterone levels in Hsd3b6−/− mice.

Based on these new data, we have added the plasma aldosterone measurements as Fig. S6 and revised the Discussion accordingly. These results further support our conclusion that the phenotypes observed in Hsd3b6−/− mice are unlikely to be secondary to systemic endocrine alterations and instead reflect the loss of local steroidogenic activity within the eyelid.
“…Plasma aldosterone levels were likewise preserved in Hsd3b6−/− mice (Fig. S6), consistent with the redundant expression of Hsd3b6 and Hsd3b1 in the adrenal gland zona glomerulosa cells [85-87].”

disp-quote.p: (d) What is the age of the mice that underwent microarray analysis? The Methods section only specifies "young" and "old" without providing the actual ages. Although the ages can be inferred from the figures, they should also be clearly stated in the Methods section.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We have now clarified the age of the mice in the Methods section. All mice used for the microarray analysis were age-matched and were 9 weeks old at the time of tissue collection (please see page 35, lines 818-819).

disp-quote.p: (e) Line 148: CD11b+ cells in the eye are usually referred to as dendritic cells derived from monocytes that function as antigen-presenting cells (APCs), rather than as phagocytes.
(f) Line 149: How was it determined that the CD38+ cells are macrophages? CD38 can also be expressed by T cells, plasma cells, NK cells, and other immune cell types.

body.p: Heeding these important instructions and based on their co-labeling with the myeloid marker CD11b, we have rewritten our Results on the cell identity of CD38 cells, as follows.

“… We also found that the myeloid cell marker CD11b stained the same cells (Fig. S2), indicating an increased number of myeloid immune cells that express CD38 in the tarsal plate of Hsd3b6−/− mice (Fig. 2E, vs. Hsd3b6+/+).”

In addition, to clarify that multiple immune cell types can contribute to CD38 expression in the tarsal plate and ocular tissues, we have extensively revised our manuscript by adding a new paragraph to the Discussion as follows.

“Secondly, the cellular identity of the CD38-expressing cells observed in the tarsal plate warrants careful interpretation. In the present study, we observed co-localization of CD38 with the myeloid marker CD11b, indicating that these cells are of myeloid origin. However, CD11b+ cells in ocular tissues such as in conjunctiva are often described as monocyte-derived dendritic cells functioning as antigen-presenting cells, rather than as classical phagocytic macrophages [95,96]. Therefore, our data do not allow us to further resolve the specific myeloid subpopulation (e.g., macrophages, dendritic cells, or other subsets) responsible for CD38 expression. In addition, CD38 is known to be expressed across multiple immune cell types, including T cells, plasma cells, and NK cells [97-99], suggesting that non-myeloid immune cells may also contribute to the overall CD38 signal in the tarsal plate. While previous studies in other tissues, such as in adipose tissue and liver [39,40], have attributed age-associated CD38 upregulation primarily to macrophages, our findings highlight the need for more precise cell-type–resolved analyses in ocular tissues. Future studies using lineage-specific markers or single-cell approaches will be required to define the exact cellular sources of CD38 and their respective contributions to NAD metabolism and inflammation in the eyelid.” Added references:

disp-quote.p: (g) LPS-induced inflammation is acute and severe and may not accurately model MGD, which is typically characterized by chronic, low-grade inflammation. It is suggested to use a more relevant model, such as benzalkonium chloride exposure or a desiccating stress chamber.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. We agree that benzalkonium chloride exposure and desiccating stress are widely used and well-established models for ocular surface inflammation and dry eye [30-35], and we have also tested these approaches in our experimental system. However, while these treatments reproducibly induced inflammatory responses in the cornea, conjunctiva, and meibomian orifice, we did not observe detectable inflammatory changes within the tarsal plate (i.e., the internal eyelid tissue containing the meibomian glands). To our knowledge, induction of inflammation in the tarsal plate by these approaches has not been reported in the literature. As such, in our current study, we adopted subcutaneous LPS injection into the eyelid. However, as noted by the reviewer, this approach represents an acute and relatively strong inflammatory stimulus and does not fully recapitulate the chronic low-grade inflammation characteristic of MGD. Please note that, by describing both the rationale and limitations of this approach, we have improved our manuscript as follows:

“Eye-drop instillation of inflammatory stimuli such as those by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or benzalkonium chloride has been shown to be effective to cause inflammation in the cornea and conjunctiva [30-35]. However, we found this approach ineffective to induce inflammation in the tarsal plate (inside the eyelid tissue). Therefore, we performed subcutaneous injection of LPS to the eyelids (see Methods).”

Methods [Page 30, lines 694-701] “LPS (Sigma) was reconstituted in saline and injected subcutaneously (5 µg/eyelid) 8 h before tissue collection for qRT-PCR analysis. LPS was administered every other day for a total of three or six doses before the measurement of meibomian NAD⁺ concentration or meibomian 3β-HSD enzymatic activity, respectively. Subcutaneous microinjection was performed using an insulin syringe (Becton Dickinson, 30G). This LPS-based approach represents an acute inflammatory stimulus and does not fully recapitulate the chronic low-grade inflammation characteristic of MGD — while it provides a practical means to induce inflammation in the tarsal plate.” Added references:
